question: What happens when you specify `environment: name: staging` in a GitLab CI job?

options.text: GitLab creates/updates a named environment with deployment history, current version, and rollback capability
options.explanation: Correct. Environment in GitLab is a living object: it stores the date, commit, and executor of each deployment and allows rollback to a previous version via the UI.

options.text: Variables from all environments become available in this job
options.explanation: The opposite: the job only receives variables tied to the specified environment in GitLab CI/CD Variables settings.

options.text: GitLab simply adds a label to the job for navigation convenience
options.explanation: This is not just a label. GitLab creates a full record in the Environments section with deployment history, rollback buttons, and a URL link.

options.text: GitLab automatically creates a corresponding branch in the repository
options.explanation: Branches and environments are independent entities. An environment is created in the Deployments section, not in the repository.

question: Why is it mandatory to specify `GIT_STRATEGY: none` in a stop job (action: stop)?

options.text: This is a GitLab CI syntax requirement — otherwise `action: stop` does not work
options.explanation: Syntactically action: stop works without GIT_STRATEGY: none, but the job would fail in practice when trying to clone a deleted branch.

options.text: Because the stop job has no access to the codebase for security reasons
options.explanation: There is no such security restriction. The problem is purely technical — the branch is already deleted by the time the stop job runs.

options.text: Because the stop job runs after the branch is deleted, and GitLab cannot clone it
options.explanation: Exactly. When an MR is merged, the branch is deleted, and the stop job runs after that. Without GIT_STRATEGY: none, the Runner tries to clone the deleted branch and fails with an error.

options.text: To speed up job execution — cloning takes extra time
options.explanation: Performance is secondary here. The main reason is that the stop job often runs after the branch is deleted, and cloning is physically impossible.

question: What is the main advantage of Blue-Green deployment over Rolling?

options.text: Blue-Green requires fewer resources since you don't need to keep two environments simultaneously
options.explanation: The opposite: Blue-Green requires twice the resources, as both environments (blue and green) must be fully deployed at the same time.

options.text: Blue-Green allows testing on real traffic before full switchover
options.explanation: This describes Canary deployment, not Blue-Green. In Blue-Green, traffic is switched entirely, not gradually.

options.text: Blue-Green guarantees that users don't see mixed API versions
options.explanation: This is a valid point, but it describes the difference from Rolling, not the main advantage. The key advantage is rollback speed — one switch vs. redeploying all instances.

options.text: Blue-Green allows instant rollback — just switch traffic back to the old environment
options.explanation: Correct. With Blue-Green, the old environment (blue) remains untouched during deployment to green. If something goes wrong — one call to update-lb.sh and traffic goes back to blue.

question: The team deploys an application to Kubernetes. On every merge to main, the new version needs to be checked on 10% of traffic before a full rollout. Which strategy is suitable?

options.text: Feature flags — hide functionality behind a flag and enable for 10% of users
options.explanation: Feature flags solve a different problem — managing functionality at the code level. They don't replace the infrastructure deployment strategy for a new image version.

options.text: Blue-Green — first deploy to green, switch 10% through the load balancer
options.explanation: Blue-Green switches traffic entirely (0% -> 100%), not gradually. For fractional traffic distribution, a different approach is needed.

options.text: Canary deploy — a separate deployment with the new version receives 10% of traffic, after verification — full rollout
options.explanation: Canary exists exactly for this. A separate deployment with a minimal number of replicas (10%) handles part of the traffic. If metrics are OK — increase replicas to 100% and remove canary.

options.text: Rolling deploy — update pods one at a time, starting with 10%
options.explanation: Rolling updates all instances sequentially without control of traffic percentage. There is no way to fix at 10% and wait for metrics verification.

question: What does `CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` mean in the context of Review Apps?

options.text: The first 8 characters of the commit SHA that triggered the pipeline
options.explanation: The commit SHA is CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA. CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG is the branch/tag name in a URL/DNS-safe format.

options.text: A unique pipeline identifier for this branch
options.explanation: The pipeline identifier is CI_PIPELINE_ID. CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG is derived from the branch/tag name.

options.text: URL-encoded branch name with / replaced by %2F
options.explanation: URL encoding with %2F is not suitable for DNS subdomain names. CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG replaces all unsafe characters with hyphens, rather than URL-encoding them.

options.text: Branch name in lowercase with unsafe characters replaced by hyphens
options.explanation: Correct. CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG transforms the branch name for use in DNS, URLs, namespace names. For example, feature/user-auth becomes feature-user-auth. Always lowercase, safe for subdomains.

question: How does `auto_stop_in: 1 week` work in the environment configuration?

options.text: Environment variables and secrets become invalid after a week
options.explanation: auto_stop_in manages the lifecycle of the environment (deployment), not the expiration of secrets or variables.

options.text: One week after the last deployment, GitLab stops the environment and launches the on_stop job
options.explanation: Correct. The timer is updated on each deployment. This prevents accumulation of abandoned review apps — if a branch is forgotten, the environment deletes itself.

options.text: One week after the environment is created, GitLab automatically launches the stop job
options.explanation: Counting starts not from creation, but from the last deployment. Each new deployment resets the timer. If a review app was deployed today, deletion will be in a week, regardless of when the environment was created.

options.text: The pipeline automatically reruns after a week to update the environment
options.explanation: auto_stop_in is a deletion timer, not a rerun schedule. For periodic runs, use scheduled pipelines.

question: In a pipeline there is a rollback job with `when: manual` and `needs: []`. What does `needs: []` mean in this context?

options.text: The job does not require any artifacts from previous jobs
options.explanation: needs: [] does indeed disable artifact downloads, but in the context of a rollback job the main effect is different — the job can be triggered manually at any time, independently, without waiting for other jobs.

options.text: The job runs only if all other jobs in the pipeline have failed
options.explanation: For running on failure, use when: on_failure. needs: [] means no dependencies, not reaction to errors.

options.text: The job can be triggered manually at any time, without waiting for other jobs in the pipeline to complete
options.explanation: Correct. needs: [] means no dependencies, so the rollback job is available for manual launch immediately, without waiting for deploy or other stages. This is critical — in an emergency you can't wait for the entire pipeline to complete.

options.text: The job does not inherit variables from previous stages
options.explanation: needs does not affect variable inheritance. Variables are available from CI/CD settings independently of needs.

question: The team wants to deploy to production only from the main branch, only manually, and only for users with the Maintainer role. Which approach to use?

options.text: Use `rules: if '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == main' when: manual` and configure Protected Environment in GitLab Settings
options.explanation: Correct. rules restricts the branch and requires manual launch, while Protected Environments in GitLab Settings allows specifying the minimum role for deploying to this environment — these are two independent levels of protection.

options.text: Add a user role check script at the start of the deploy job via CI_GITLAB_USER_LOGIN
options.explanation: This is a fragile and unreliable solution. The correct path is built-in GitLab mechanisms: Protected Environments, which check the role declaratively, without custom scripts.

options.text: Specify `only: - main` and `when: manual` in the job — that is enough
options.explanation: only: main and when: manual restrict the branch and require manual launch, but do not restrict the user role. A Developer would also be able to launch the deploy.

options.text: Create a separate project in GitLab only for production deploys with restricted access
options.explanation: Creating a separate project is an excessive architectural complication. GitLab provides Protected Environments specifically to solve this task within a single project.

question:
What is wrong with the following configuration?

```yaml
deploy:
  script:
    - docker build -t myapp:latest .
    - docker push myapp:latest
    - deploy myapp:latest
```

options.text: The image should be built in a separate build stage, not in deploy
options.explanation: Separating into stages is good practice, but not the main problem. The key issue is the inability to rollback.

options.text: docker build needs to be run with --no-cache for reproducibility
options.explanation: --no-cache slows the build and does not solve the rollback problem. This is not the error in this configuration.

options.text: There is no environment: name — GitLab will not track deployments
options.explanation: The absence of environment: name is a shortcoming, but not a critical problem in terms of deployment reliability. More critical is the lost ability to rollback.

options.text: The latest tag is overwritten on every deployment — there is no way to rollback to a previous version
options.explanation: Correct. After each deployment, the old latest is lost forever. The correct pattern: SHA tag for each commit, previous tag for the previous version, stable for the current production.

question: A developer set up Review Apps. After merging the MR, the environment is not deleted. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Forgot to specify `GIT_STRATEGY: none` in the stop job, so the job fails when trying to clone the deleted branch
options.explanation: A classic mistake. After merge, the branch is deleted. The stop job launches and tries to clone a nonexistent branch — fails with an error, the environment remains in a stopped state without executing the cleanup script.

options.text: Kubernetes namespace cannot be deleted via GitLab CI — a separate webhook is needed
options.explanation: Kubernetes namespace is perfectly deletable via kubectl in GitLab CI. The problem is that the stop job fails before executing this command.

options.text: auto_stop_in is not specified — GitLab does not know when to delete the environment
options.explanation: auto_stop_in is an optional setting for automatic deletion by timer. For deletion on MR close, on_stop is used, and its successful execution depends on GIT_STRATEGY.

options.text: rules instead of only/except — GitLab does not launch the stop job on merge
options.explanation: rules works correctly with Review Apps and on_stop. This is not the cause of the cleanup non-execution problem.

question: How do CI/CD variables tied to a specific environment in GitLab Settings behave in the pipeline?

options.text: Available only in jobs where `environment: name` matches the variable's binding name
options.explanation: Correct. This is a key feature of Environment Variables in GitLab — secret isolation. The DATABASE_URL variable for production is only available in the deploy-production job, not in deploy-staging or test.

options.text: Variables with environment binding have priority over regular variables only in the deploy stage
options.explanation: Priority is determined by level (instance -> group -> project), not by stage. Environment variables are only available in matching jobs — this is about scope, not priority.

options.text: Available in all jobs of the pipeline, regardless of environment: name in the job
options.explanation: If production secrets were available everywhere, this would violate the principle of least privilege. GitLab specifically limits their visibility.

options.text: You must explicitly specify the variable name in `environment: variables:` to use it
options.explanation: Variables bound to an environment in the GitLab UI are automatically injected into the job — no additional configuration is needed in .gitlab-ci.yml.

question: The team uses Rolling deploy to update 4 application instances. After updating the 2nd instance, a critical error is discovered. What is the fastest way to return the service to a stable state?

options.text: Wait for the rolling update to finish and then deploy the previous version
options.explanation: Waiting means updating 2 more instances with the broken version. The right thing is to stop the rolling update as early as possible.

options.text: Stop the pipeline and manually launch the previous image on the 2 updated instances
options.explanation: Manual work on instances is slow and non-reproducible. Better to use automated rollback via CI/CD.

options.text: Stop the current pipeline and launch the rollback job with the previous image SHA for all instances
options.explanation: Correct. A rollback job with when: manual and needs: [] can be launched immediately. It applies the previous stable image to all 4 instances — faster and more reliable than manual actions.

options.text: Press the Re-deploy button in GitLab UI for the previous deployment in the Environments section
options.explanation: Re-deploy via GitLab UI is a working option, but it launches the entire pipeline with the previous commit, which may take time. A dedicated rollback job without extra stages is faster.

question: What is the "mixed versions problem" in Rolling deploy and when is it critical?

options.text: Different application instances run different versions simultaneously — critical when there are incompatible changes to the API or database schema
options.explanation: Exactly. If v2 changes a table format in the DB, and v1 writes in the old format — there will be corruption. Or if v2 changes the REST API contract — clients served by v1 will get an unexpected response. Solution: backward-compatible migrations and API versioning.

options.text: The problem only occurs with horizontal scaling of more than 10 instances
options.explanation: The mixed versions problem occurs with any number of instances (even 2). The 10-instance threshold is a made-up restriction.

options.text: Different versions of configuration files on different servers — easily solved through centralized config management
options.explanation: Configuration files are not the main problem. Critical is the simultaneous operation of incompatible code and data schema versions.

options.text: Different Docker image versions in the Registry — old images take up space
options.explanation: Storing multiple image versions is normal and needed for rollback. The mixed versions problem is about runtime behavior, not storage.

question: In GitLab CI you need to set up deployment so that the `deploy-production` job runs only after a successful `deploy-staging`, only from the main branch, and only manually. Which configuration is correct?

options.text: `when: manual` + `needs: [deploy-staging]` without rules — needs already guarantees running after staging
options.explanation: needs guarantees execution order, but does not restrict the branch. Without rules, the job will run when deploying from any branch.

options.text: `when: manual` + `only: [main]` + `needs: [deploy-staging]`
options.explanation: only/except and rules cannot be used together with needs in modern pipelines. You need to use rules instead of only.

options.text: `stage: deploy-production` + `only: [main]` — stage guarantees order after deploy-staging
options.explanation: stages only provide sequential order. The job in stage deploy-production will run after the deploy-staging stage, but without when: manual — automatically.

options.text: `rules: [{if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"', when: manual}]` + `needs: [deploy-staging]`
options.explanation: Correct. rules with the branch condition and when: manual set the launch condition. needs: [deploy-staging] guarantees that the job will be available only after a successful deploy-staging.

question: A Review App is configured with `on_stop: stop-review`. In which cases will GitLab automatically launch the stop-review job?

options.text: Only when manually pressing the Stop button in the Environments section
options.explanation: Manual stop is one way, but not the only one. GitLab can launch stop automatically in certain events.

options.text: Only when auto_stop_in expires — on merge you need to manually launch stop
options.explanation: GitLab automatically launches stop-review on branch deletion, which usually happens immediately after merging an MR. This is a key Review Apps feature.

options.text: On branch deletion (merge or delete) and on auto_stop_in timer expiration
options.explanation: Correct. GitLab automatically launches the on_stop job: on branch deletion (after MR merge), on auto_stop_in timer expiration, and on manual stop via the UI. This ensures automatic resource cleanup.

options.text: On every new deployment to the same environment — the old one automatically stops
options.explanation: A new deployment updates the environment, but does not stop it. stop-review is a separate action for resource deletion, it is not triggered on update.
